projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Steve M. Hegedus was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Mr. Steve Hegedus. Mr. Hegedus served in the US Army with the 11th Airborne Division, 511th parachute infantry. Steve's highest rank was staff sergeant and he served in the Pacific theater. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at myh ome in metro Ohio on January 14, 2003. Los Angeles Times reporter Steve Brown was also present as Steve Hegedus was 78 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: I've only lived in three houses in my life. When I was a kid growing up I lived in the Hungarian neighborhood called Buckeye Road in Cleveland, Ohio and then I was drafted in, I went to the Army on January 15, 1943 and I got out of the Army three years and one day later, January 15, 1946 and I've only two claims to fame for being in the Army. One, I was one of the very few, maybe not the only American soldier burned with mustard gas and I have two marks there like a figure eight, one is the size of a quarter and the other a half dollar on my left rear hip. Want to hear that story?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yes, tell me how that happened.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Okay. And the other claim to fame is, I was in the same squad, same platoon, same company, my entire three years in the Army. My squad leader, Sergeant McGuire (ph), at whose funeral I gave a nice eulogy and said he was a soldier's soldier and a sergeant's sergeant and I could never figure out how a young kid 21 years old had such a leadership ability. So one day at Camp McCall, North Carolina, we did two things as part of our schooling. We went a little bit out of camp to the right kind of topography and we dug some foxholes and then an Army tank appeared and we got down into our holes and the tank ran over us. But when the tank spun around on the hole, nobody was in it and they wanted to show you what that tank could do and what you could do to the tank such as if you had like bubble gum you could stick it to the bottom or something.

And when it spun around on this one foxhole it like crushed it so if you had been in there that would have been the last bubble gum you ever ate. So at the next part of that class was an exhibit by somebody, an officer from the chemical warfare service and he had several things painted green like an Army helmet and a couple of boards and then he had this chemical which was mustard gas and he put it on the helmet and on these boards and it turned red. So if you are ever walking along and everything starts to turn red, you know you're in trouble. So evidently the guy next to me dropped it in the sand next to me and I must have sat in it because that night we went on an all-night march and as we were starting out when it was just getting dark, that darn canteen was rubbing my left hip so I just moved it a little. Well, that canteen had been bobbing along like waltzing Matilda for six months and it never bothered me, so I moved it again and it started to hurt. By the time we got back in about three, four in the morning, it really hurt and it was all red. So the next morning, it was two nice circles the size which I just told you, blisters.

So the sergeant looked at it, he said, you know, you better go on sick call, it looks like a spider bite. So I went on sick call and they looked at my rear end and an officer came in and said, where were you, he never saw anything like it. It's a spider bite, everybody said. And so somehow or other as he's walking out, I said, oh, I was at the mustard gas demonstration yesterday. He spun around on his heel and he says, what? And so I told him, and he told the sergeant, you know, don't do anything, don't cut that blister open like they were doing to everybody else that morning, not with mustard gas, I guess, with just regular walking blisters. And then I had to explain again what happened. And he says, stay right where you are. So there I am, I'm lying on a cot with my pants pulled down and pretty soon. They started to come in and everybody looking at me by rank. First all of the medical sergeants were brought in and told to look at this, it's probably mustard gas. Then they brought every medic who was on duty came in. Then they brought in some guys from the base hospital. Then the division surgeon came in and they were all looking at me and treating me nice, bringing me juice or whatever.

And finally, some guy must have flown in because by now it's noon, must have flown in from the Washington DC, you know, chemical warfare or medics or something. So he looked. So then our division, regimental surgeon said, told some captain, get a clean scalpel and some clean cotton balls and puncture that skin and save that liquid. So that's what they did. So that was my second claim to fame. Everybody from Washington DC down to the corporal looking at my rear end. And I do have two nice, a figure eight of that stuff. So I guess that mustard gas works. All right, are you ready? By the way, before you go you're going to tell me your name again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any odd stories from training that you remember?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: I'm not trying to think of them right now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: But I will.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go wherever you want to go.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Okay, this is sort of good, oh, what a battle this is going to be. It's Valentine's Day 1945 near Pasai (ph), Rizal (ph), Luzon in the Philippines. Let's see, Pasai might be like a county and Rizal might be like a state what we call in this country and it was about 30 miles southeast of Manila, we never got to Manila, beautiful, bright, sunny day which we really appreciated after living in the mud of Leyte for 37 days. The story of the leeches on Leyte is another story. But a major came down from Division and he made a sand map which included a helmet to mean the hill about a thousand yards away, you know, three football fields away across this hard rice paddy and then up that hill are pill boxes and the Japs, assuming. Okay.

So, and then there was a piece of bamboo, a nice, straight piece of bamboo, that was the railroad track just below going up the hill. And in front of that or in the middle of that field was a great big American artillery piece left over from, you know, when the Japs took over in 1941. So that will fit into this story also. And then cutting across that railroad track and from where we were in a big ditch, there was a road, a pretty good road. So when we heard that we were going to have this big battle in a day or two -- oh, the reason it was going to be a big battle, B Company was going to on our left, they would be guiding on that road and then an Army tank was going to come and help us. Well, that made us feel good because we never even saw one over there. So our sergeant, DuFresne (ph), who was so GI, the last four numbers of his serial number were 1776. Now, now how could you beat that? And he was sort of an amateur historian.

And after we each went up a couple at a time and viewed this sand map, he said, you know, this is like the battle of Agincourt in France, it was a big battle, and he says, Shakespeare wrote about it and he said it was something about, it's going to be a bloody battle but you and your grandchildren will be proud that you fought there. Whether you live or die, they'll always say you fought the battle of Agincourt on St. Crispin's Day.

So before we get into the actual battle, no battle is won or lost on the day of the battle, it's won or lost six months or two years before, like who said that the battle of Waterloo was run on the playing fields of Eaton, do you know? Supposedly you learn competition, killing and stuff like that elsewhere. Or you could even be married. So any way, I have to backtrack and say one of the best things that ever happened to our unit, the 511th parachute infantry, we trained as a unit for over a year and a half up to that point from about January of '43 to now this was '45, same guys, and the Army learned or realized after Vietnam when these guys, eight guys would be brought in on a helicopter, they jump out and before they shut off the rotors, eight guys would be replaced.

They never saw each other, learned their names or anything else and sometimes guys in one foxhole next to another didn't know anything about their fellow soldier there. But we did, you know, we worked together, sweated together, cursed the Army together. So there we are and we knew what we were there for. We knew we could do that job. So you have to go back to when we were formed there, Camp McCall and we went to parachute training in May of '43 and then we started to do things like, oh, what do you call that, basic training, that's learning your basic skills, usually rifle.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What division was this?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Oh, yes, here's a present for you. It was the 511th parachute infantry regiment, 11th airborne division.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is for me?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow, neat. Thank you.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Then after that, then you go into squad training. By the way, am I allowed to say this on this TV? Every division has, you know, a symbol or a shoulder patch. The 17th Airborne has the talon of an eagle. The 101st has the eagle's head and we used to call ours if you look at it, the flying red asshole. You can edit that out if you want.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, that's the kind of stuff that's important to remember.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: We used to say, what's the last thing you see when a bird is flying away from you, yeah. So then we went from these squad problems to platoon and some of that stuff for platoon we went to Fort Bragg, walked to Fort Bragg because Camp McCall was just a chunk of land cut out of Fort Bragg. Fort Bragg used to be the biggest in area of all of the military bases and Fort Benning had the most people there. It was the largest of both of those and Fort Bragg was one of the two or three artillery practice places. And all over there were signs, do not touch, what do you call that stuff, do not touch artillery, whatever it is. There were big shells stuck in trees just laying upside down, just laying there on the ground.

Well, you know, guys had to do something so they found a mortar shell and I saw them actually playing with it back at camp. Don't shake your head, nobody got hurt. They would throw the darn thing up, who can throw it the highest and it always turned over and landed on its nose, right? Well, one night they were playing cards, must have been right after payday and this darn thing which had been thrown up and down and hit and everything else, it fell off a footlocker, we're talking 18 inches and it went off. Nobody got hurt, one guy had just put his head on his pillow and a big hung of shrapnel went right where his head had been and embedded itself in the barracks wall. Life is nothing but luck, you know. You could walk out of here tomorrow and get hit by a truck.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's hear the odd thing.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: The odd thing about what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were just saying, do you want to hear an odd thing.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Okay, for lunch that day we had hot dogs, a very mediocre lunch. When we were in the plane going to jump there in Florence, South Carolina, it was a very bumpy ride. Some guys started to throw up. And, you know, that's contagious, one guy does it and the next. Maybe just the sound (indicating) starts it in you. I swear to God when they passed that bucket around to me where everybody was throwing up, there was a whole wiener in there. How could anybody, not a half, it was a whole wiener. Boy, they must have been hungry. Okay, then we had division maneuvers. Then we were going to move the whole division to Camp Polk, Louisiana where big maneuvers was going on. We didn't jump down there, we just walked and we were chasing some Army division.

We were on foot, they were in trucks. How stupid can that be. But I stayed behind at Camp McCall to help clean up. I think it was one guy from each barracks and then we got on the train and we were going to Camp Polk. The train was in an accident. We hit something. And believe it or not, my feet were facing forward and nothing happened to me. I wrote a letter to the White House and said if the President ever travels, let him travel feet first, you know, on the train. Two trains, what do you call those, cars in front of us were the prisoners from our stockade, probably some bad guys were in there, but any way, they had to call the MPs and they had to disconnect the windows, take the windows out and everybody being guarded and then hand some of these prisoners out on stretchers out those windows. Then everything else was okay. Want to hear another train story?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: This one is funny but almost disastrous. As we were going from Camp Polk to the West Coast, at that moment we didn't know where we were going, were we going to Europe or Japan. So we were going from Camp Polk naturally north. And then all of a sudden we swung west and we knew we were going to the Pacific. So a couple of times our car stopped right in the middle of a small town. That's the way it was out west. The train station was, grade crossing was right there. So we were always hungry and we saw a drug store as close as we are to that garage from the train. So we said, next time we see something like that, we're getting off, we're going to jump off this train and buy something, gum, candy.

And one time we saw a bakery. We said, the next bakery is ours. Oh, by the way, we had been read, what article of war is it, called the 96th to the 98th, as of this day, as of this day that they read you this, if you are AWOL, you are considered a deserter and there's the old firing squad threat. So I should have listened. So we stopped in the middle of this town in Iowa, it's getting dusk already. And Frank and I jump off. We run up the street maybe a hundred feet, we bust into this bakery, there's these old grandmothers here. And don't forget, all of our insignia were off, not even rank was on, our trousers were over our paratroop boots so somebody couldn't tell, this was a really big secret.

But a lot of these women's husbands worked for the railroad so when we go in, we would say, we're on that troop train, could we go ahead of you, please? One sweet little old grandma gave me a cake box with a cake in it. She says, my grandson is in Europe and the other women just stepped aside me and said, throw all those doughnuts in the bag. And we then put like 40 dollars down on the counter and said, just give us whatever you got.

And one of the women said, I'll bet you're from the 11th Airborne, they are supposed to be going through here and when we got to California they were at least a dozen wives from some of the officers in our regiment. Any way, Frank had his armload of bakery and he was waiting outside and all of a sudden inside he said, the train's moving. So I just grabbed whatever I had and ran down. And like I said, it was only 200 feet to that train, and you can't believe how fast that train can start going very, very fast.

So I got down to the train platform, I turn right and I'm racing the train now and worrying about that 98th article of war, the firing squad, the stockade, murder and everything else. So at olympian speed I'm running down this train platform. Remember OJ, how he used to run over the, leap over the, well, I did all of that, carts and suitcases and everything. And then all of a sudden I realized this cement platform has to end and there's not very much light and out of the corner of my eye the train is going as fast as I'm running. So at the very end I dropped all of the bakery and made a super dive. And I see the train going by and by just pure luck I put my hands out and I'm seeing myself under the wheels, but the wheels were already past me and I dove at that platform. Remember Harry Truman speaking on the platform?

Well, my hand, my right hand landed on some kind of pipe and I held on. And my left hand, the fingernails were digging into the steel. There must have been a minute crack in that steel because my fingernails were hanging on to that. Then my legs are flailing away in the back and my ankle hit something, a semaphore post, something but that hurt like hell, and that almost turned me sideways and then on top of that my right shin bone, you can see the scar and the indent, it hit the sharp corner of the step of this caboose. That hurt like hell.

So I don't know what to do, the train is going faster and faster and in my mind I was thinking if I let go, I'd never heard of rent a car but that's what I was thinking of in those days, I don't even have a driver's license, I don't know how to drive but here you are always trying to out fake the Army. And I figured, oh, if I could get a car, if I let go and I'll get a car and I'll drive to wherever this train is going, yeah. That was sort of stupid. And the next thing I know, old sarge has a hold of my, not me, of my coveralls, the sleeve and he was like bending over to me and he says, just don't let go and I says (indicating) and then pretty soon good buddy Frank, late of the bakery delivery business, he's grabbing my, some part of my clothing down around my waist.
And so they pulled me up a little bit. And when I sat down leaning against the car, I said, I think I hurt my leg. So I looked at my shins and there was a lot of blood dripping into that, my boot.

So they called the medic and he came and he didn't even come out on the platform. He says, you know, he says, I don't know what happened out here and I don't want to know but if I do know I'd have to write it down. So he says, I tell you what, Sarge, tell me what you see. And sarge says, well, I see a lot of blood. He says, okay, open my bag here, and it was either cotton or big gauze and he says, just press it on there and see what you can see. So sarge says, looks like a lot of blood coming from his shin bone. Okay, the medic says, there's a bottle of alcohol in the upper left or something. So they put that on there. And it hurt like hell and the only salvation was they did save me a piece of lemon merengue pie. That was pretty darn good. And you know how we thanked that medic? We let him die out in the sun at Fort McKinley. So that was not very nice. Okay, we got on the boat, we went to New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: About when was that?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: May '44. We better get up to the battle of Fort McKinley and forget New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: If there's anything you want to touch on with New Guinea, we got lots of tape.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: On New Guinea, for this one time we had some classes or B Company against A Company, we would be hiding in this tall grass, taller than you, called Kunai (ph) grass. So for this whole week, all our exercises are in this Kunai grass. All of a sudden everybody panics, the medics found out that Kunai grass is where the typhus bug lives, yeah, so no more Kunai grass. And another thing that happened, somebody shot a wild boar in the hills of New Guinea. Well, our medics and a lot of the guys were just farm boys and they knew what to do so they cut it open and examined the, hey, anything in the wild is healthy so they cut the head off of that and they cooked that wild boar and I remember I was in the chow line and there's that boar's head sitting there and the ax which was used to cut the head off.

So I said, I want to see how hard that is, so I took the ax and I hit that boar right between the eyes and it was like hitting concrete. That's how hard it was. Oh, yeah, one other thing that shows you I'm lucky. We were way up in the mountains of New Guinea -- by the way, after we had some time to, by time, I mean weeks, the guys were going out exploring a little more. So they went up way in the hills and they found an airplane, an American plane that had been shot down two or three years before and never found.

It was in the jungle, in the hills. So they stole all that they could from the pilot, you know, bracelets and everything and then they reported it. There was nothing left, nothing of value. So this one time we're way up in the hills, maybe two or 3,000 feet high and we stopped for a minute and there were these vines, there were two vines that looked the same. One, if you cut it, it had like a greenish viscous fluid that was a poison. I saw some guys who drank some or ingested it somehow and they were berserk, they were crazy. The other vine looked just like it but when you cut that in half it was red and there was water in it.

If you took a, say you cut it here and then just made a slash up there, there would be enough water to fill a canteen cup and that was good, potable water. And I think I have a nice scar here where I hit with a machete, I went like that and the blade went down the vine and right on to my hand here somewhere.

Any way, that was very good food for the leeches. They liked any kind of mucous membrane. So the class clown, me and Frank, we had to swing out on that vine which was 200 feet high. So somebody goes out first and I'm next and I swing out real slow. I don't know what these words about pendulums mean but what do you call that when you swing out and you swing back. Any way, when you are swinging out, I bet I was like 200 feet on the vine and at least 200 feet over the jungle floor.

And I swung back, I didn't pay any attention in high school physics, but nothing swings back as far as when you let it go. So here I'm swinging back and I realize I'm not going to make that same place so I let go, I fell about eight feet, nothing's wrong except the vine broke at the top. And thank God I had my helmet liner on because it came down just rip-rapping me on the head and if that had broken three seconds before, they'd still be looking for me. So that was another New Guinea story.

Okay, where did we go from New Guinea? We went by boat up to Leyte. That was a very wet place, you know, just an island over there in the Pacific. But it sure was wet and then the farther we got up into the mountains, the wetter it was and the clouds would be below us. Well, a lot of things happened on Leyte. One thing that I did see, first, we were in the hills 37 days. There was a three-day period when we didn't eat, not anything, nothing. Then we got some kind of food. Then there was five days when we didn't eat, not a thing. We were thinking about eating the bark off a tree. Somebody did find some sweet potatoes, they ate that. The first thing I had to eat after that five days was one K ration dog biscuit. You know what that is? You know what a regular dog biscuit is, they made these things for the Army and they were supposed to be very nutritious, greens and stuff.

We were carrying a wounded guy up to a so-called hospital and there was a machine gun covering the trail and there was a K ration dog biscuit lying in the mud and I asked those guys could I have it and they said yeah. The guy we were carrying up was a good kid from southern Ohio and his leg was blown off in the middle of the night by either our own grenade or the Japs, one of the two. But we kept putting that blown off foot back on the stretcher hoping that, you know, the doctors could do a miracle but he didn't make it. Let's see, the mud, that's another story. So we finally came -- and then there was another three-day period where we had nothing to eat. So the Army owes me eight and three, eleven meals, eleven days of meals.

How do I collect? What department do I write? So any way, it was probably the best Christmas we ever had when we came out of the hills and brought our wounded and the guys with crutches, everything home made, poncho. You know what a poncho is? We made stretchers out of that and some sticks, poles, trees, got them all out of there. Then we went by boat to Mindoro. What a blessing, hot and dry, wasn't very far away and we couldn't believe it. Some Air Force, there was an Air Force runway there and there was vitamins on the table. You know, for a guy that didn't eat right, vitamins, we couldn't believe it. So any way, we flew from Mindoro and now we're going to go up to Luzon. So February 4th we landed oh, about 50 miles, no, it was 50 kilometers, 37 miles south of Manila on a place called Tagaytay Ridge. You know the Philippines or the whole, it's called what, the ring of fire, the rim of fire, all of those places where there's volcanos all around the Pacific there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Well, this was one of them. So we landed, nothing spectacular, it was a routine drop although as soon as I hit the ground I heard this parachute coming down, it didn't open up, this was an equipment chute, these parachutes were colored, I'm going to just guess and say red for medical supplies, green for ammo and blue for bookkeeping, you know, something different. And here this thing came down and it like makes this noise (indicating), they call that a cigarette roll, I don't know why. And there were also some cases where, between Pop Franklin (ph) and X line, one of them landed on the chute of the other in midair and so the upper guy's chute collapsed and he slipped off the good chute and the guy down below grabbed him as he went by and they landed okay and they are both still living today. So we assembled immediately on the road, and like I said, we saw a sign that said 50 kilometers and some college smart guy figured out, you know, five-eighths or something like that and we were ready to go in one minute. Some guy hollered from across the road and hollered, hey, come on over here.

And so we went over there and evidently the land had uplifted a million years ago like this so this Tagaytay Ridge was this original up here and this was a huge drop of about 2,000 feet and what was at the bottom was Lake Taal, T-A-A-L and in the middle of Lake Taal was the remains of a volcano and to me, a kid who only saw one National Geographic in my life before then this was like seeing National Geographic in color. So we all looked and then when somebody said, hey, it's 37 miles to Manila, we said, let's go and had no doubt we could make it by at least sundown or something. But another lucky thing happened. From where we were, walking to Manila, there was a slight downhill. Boy, does that make a difference than walking uphill.

And then the next good thing, we saw a fancy cart. It was not even as big as this table. It was painted white with a nice design on it. Around here it would be the kind of cart like a wheelbarrow almost where someone would have planted flowers in up here. So we put all of our extra machine gun, boxes full of machine gun ammo which would have been easier than carrying it, maybe they even put the mortar on it. Well, at that same time, a lot of our forces or the rest of the division landed about 30, 40 miles more south of us at a place called Nasugbao (ph). So those big ships where the front comes down, what do you call those, LSTs?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: LSTs, I think.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Those trucks were all loaded with food, ammo and medical supplies and stuff. So they had hit that beach at that time and were hoping that they would not face any opposition, you know, to get up to where we were. So they did, they got to Tagaytay Ridge and they started to unload their stuff and then the empty trucks came more toward Manila Bay and picked us up. And since we were the first Americans that these Japs, I mean, Filipinos saw, they, all of a sudden they came out with bananas, I was on the left front fender and they handed me a lot of the stuff and I just handed it back but they also dug out some bonded booze, maybe it was in the ground for four years, but that went back and that did not last long. They drank it and threw the bottles overboard.

So then by then it was getting to be almost dusk and we got out of the truck. And, oh, I forgot one thing. Somewhere between Tagaytay Ridge and where we landed, we passed some dead American soldiers. We found out later they were from F Company and they had been like path finders and they had engaged in a big firefight on this road. Fortunately, they won. But any way, there were a couple of our first dead guys on Luzon we saw. So near dusk we got out and I guess we were being shot at and they told us, everybody over on the left side of the road. Well, about one minute later, somebody saw somebody behind a row of houses and they shot them.

The story I heard, that that was the division chief of staff. What he was doing behind there, we have no idea but then at a reunion maybe 20 years ago, I think that was at Fort Benning, one of the guys in E or F Company said it couldn't have been, that this colonel died and they said he was in a Jeep and this or that happened so another one of those mysteries. So by then we were getting shelled and we came to this small town called Paranokway (ph) right by a little tiny river where they made boats and that will be in this story later.

It was a bright, starry night. I don't know if there was a moon but I know it was bright and we were only ten yards from Manila Bay. We were the left flank of the whole thing and there was a church right there. So any way, we said, looking up at that church steeple, we said, you know, that would be the perfect place for a Jap sniper or spotter to be. And sure enough, we were getting artillery raining right down on us and one of the officers says dig in, wonderful, I'm on a concrete sidewalk, dig in. So pretty soon, believe it or not, General Swing (ph), our division commander, came by in a Jeep. And the reason we didn't cross this little bridge on this little river, it had a great big two or 300 pound bomb stuck right in the middle. They had dug some cement out of the bridge and there was a bomb sitting there. I think it was an American airplane, maybe they saved that since Pearl Harbor. So we said, yeah, I'll bet you there's a guy up there spotting.

And at that time the second platoon was on Manila Bay and we're being shelled and one of the sergeants after looking things over, he says, no, move that machine gun from there to here and we'll have better cross coverage and all of that. So they did and one minute later an artillery shell came and landed in or near Sergeant Forrester (ph) and he lost his leg. And that sergeant at a reunion about 10 or 15, 20 years ago said, you know, he always blames himself for Sergeant Forrester losing his leg. And we had to tell him, that's what sergeants and lieutenants are for. If you weren't going to do that, the general doesn't need you. Will you expect him to tell you how to place your machine guns?

So any way, I don't know, can I use the word assuaged his blame? So any way, the next morning we were given the order to go check out that church. But before we could, boom, boom, there were two shots of a big gun, a big rifle like a 20 millimeter and there was an officer and Lieutenant Galligan (ph) and I don't know what the sergeant's name, they were standing in the doorway of that church, you know like you just come out of that church on Sunday morning, they are standing there, the sun is shining, it's dry, it's nice, boom, it got both of them. No, I think it was two shots.

So then we went into the church. And the Filipino churches had no pews, evidently you stood. So one group went down the left side, one squad on the right and then there's the altar and then behind the altar is going to be the steps up to the steeple. So one guy is walking down the right side and he motions everybody to stop. And there's a fresh turd behind the altar. So the name of this story is the tale of the telltale turd. So he signals his buddy and the buddy comes and they look and there's a Jap standing there as close as I am, easy, to that car but he's at a disadvantage, he's on the left side and his gun is on his right, not hip, on the floor and the one guy, American, he clicks off his safety because he's going to shoot this guy.

And the Jap hears that and so does everybody else and the Jap looks around and this guy told me and he says, I can still see his face. But he was at a disadvantage. No matter what he did, he had to turn three-quarters of the way around, if he turned to the right or to the left. So by the time everybody made up their mind, this guy shot the Jap and blew his brains out. But when the lieutenant heard that click, he says, goddamn it, now who did what. And as he's coming over to chew out some asses on this side, the brains flew past him and he toned down his anger.

But then he said, Sergeant DuFresne, take two men and go up to the top of that steeple. To me, that is one of the bravest things. Can you imagine going up, you are helpless, going up those steps, but there was nobody there, just Mr. Pooper.

So, all right, that was that for the second day. We're still a little bit far, we're about five miles from Fort McKinley. So we started to go out every day, somebody went out on patrols, we'd go this way, that way, up the beach. And at sometime at Camp McCall, I had a good chance to goof off by going to bazooka school. So we did get special food or something that whole week. So all of a sudden they are looking for two bazooka men. So my friend Nick and I are looking for Kwietkowski (ph) and Makarevich (ph) because they were the other two bazooka men but they were already both wounded on Leyte so they are going, we're next, Nick and I. So we got, they gave us a bazooka and we went on a, two or three miles down the road toward Fort McKinley and didn't see anything. So when we came back, we were sitting around. We made a little K ration lunch and, boom, out of nowhere, one artillery shot landed. There were like ten of us sitting around this big. We were sitting on, what do you call when you build a boat and you let it slide into the water, is there such a word as the ways?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The ways?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: W-A-Y, where that ship slides down the ways, did you ever hear that word?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-mm.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Any way, this is where they make boats or repair them and that's what we were sitting on and this shell landed right in the middle of us, blew us all backwards and all of a sudden Nick said, I got hit in the leg. So he had a real bad wound above the knee and he lost his leg. So then a couple of days later, it was Lincoln's birthday, February 12th and we left Perinokway and went up to Pasai, that was only a couple of miles and then from Pasai, the road takes off to the right, right to Fort McKinley. So we spent one night, that must have been February 12th or 13th. And then about like I said, a day or two later we, boy, it took this long to get to Fort McKinley? Boy, what you guys been doing? So that's when the next day was Valentine's Day and that's when the major came down and now we pick up the story of the sand map. And okay.

They told us what we're going to do, we're going to walk all the way across this hard rice paddy. There's a railroad track on an embankment and you get over that and there's where the pill boxes are. Okay. So the night of the 13th, it was another moonlit night, I did not see this because I was facing the wrong way. I was what we call, you know, a rear guard but not walking, we were in foxholes and I was facing the way we had come. Oh, yeah, wait, we have to do something else. February 13th we start out walking toward Fort McKinley and, you know, with very good Army, what would you call it, training, we were the proper distance apart, they were always telling me, don't bunch up, don't bunch up.

So we were the nice distance apart. Pretty soon we started to get shelled. I ended up on the left side, not of the road, five yards off the road and the right side was getting shelled more, I don't know why. But my friend Jim Doyle who still lives near Philadelphia near New Jersey, a shell landed real close to him and he said it actually pushed his face into the dirt and Sergeant Taylor ended up sort of on top of him and he looked toward him and he says, that leg instead of being like this, it was like -- any way, Sergeant Taylor took the brunt of that explosion. And then Doyle went to the hospital. But right after that, we're still, you know, walking, and I swear to God I saw an artillery shell in the air, as much as I would see a long pass and it landed and it didn't go off. So I had the machine gun on my shoulder.

I said, I'm going to go see that so I went over there, this was either quicksand or, do you know what a pig wallow is? You do? It's a muddy spot that the farmers make and the pigs wallow in it to keep the flies off of them. But this was not for pigs, this was for, not caribou, in America we have caribou that look like deer. Over there, this is a caribow (ph) which is a water buffalo and I have heard they are mean and they have some horns but not much. And maybe it was either quicksand or the caribow, caribow wallowed in there. So I saw the hole where that shell landed. I'm admiring it and I realize I'm sinking. I can't get out.

So by this time almost everybody had passed me. So Sergeant Pelster is looking not for me but for the machine gun, good friend from Chicago, all city basketball player. So he comes back and he says, come on, get out of there, he says, give me the machine gun. I says, no, get me out of here first. So he picks some grass or whatever and he puts it down and he says, here, stand on this. Well, that was impossible. So he reached down and I handed him the machine gun and he sort of pulled me out. So I got out, I'm all stinky, smelly from this grayish looking mud and we are continuing on and then I see about 50 yards ahead of me they have all stopped at the edge of this rice paddy and they are in this big ditch, you know, it's about five feet high and wider than your arms.

And the shells are still coming. So I ran, I made the ditch. And I thought I was the last one but here comes, I don't want to use this guy's real name, sometime I'll tell you why, I'll give him the name, I'll say Silver, here comes Silver, he's running and he gets a big shell right in the chest. And I could see his face take on a different shape or, you know, awareness and he takes about two or three more steps, maybe it was his momentum and then he landed right almost with his face in the ditch.

So we looked at him, he's foaming blood at the mouth so we took off his pack and Ralph says, open the pack, what we call a musette bag. Today it might be called, what, a backpack. But any way, so we opened it up and there were the shards of a bottle of good whiskey. And Ralph says, I own half that bottle, that son of a gun, I told him I wanted to carry it. So any way, by the time we cut his coat open he was really breathing blood and foam out of his chest.

There was nothing, I don't even think a surgeon could have saved him. So that was the end of him. So that night, I'm telling you, I didn't see this, I was given a position to face the back. All of a sudden Sergeant Pelster (ph) is coming back and he says, hold your fire, hold your fire and another act of bravery, if you can imagine in the darkness him going to this B Company on the left and telling them hold your fire, anything that moved should have been shot. I didn't know what this is all about. And the next thing all hell breaks loose, mortars, gunfire, machine gunfire, a company of Japs walks right down the road. They had been watching us all day.

They were shooting at us all day. Didn't they know where we were? They were marching three abreast and I guess they were going to go back down and cause some trouble. Usually they would, some of them would be carrying a shaped charge. Do you know what a shaped charge is? Okay, it's cone-shaped and hollow on the inside and this is all mathematically figured out that this is an explosive and when it explodes the shape of the hole makes the force concentrated to a point like a flashlight beam. And that is what our bazooka shells do.

The bazooka shell, the first half is empty and the second half is the shaped charge and the concentration of the force of that shaped charge on a tank will blow through six inches of armor plate. So these Japs had broken through. Now everybody is shooting at everybody else. The Japs on the right side I know, one of them fell in the hole with an American and the American had a hand grenade and he held it on the Jap's back and it isn't one of those stories where he blew his hand off, he let go at the last second, killed the Jap. Another one had his bayonet on, and the Jap landed on it and the Jap is still alive. But he was impaled and the guy pulled the trigger and that makes a mess.

And another guy about three days later, he's cleaning his rifle and he says, well, I'll be damned, look at that and on the butt of his rifle was a Jap's eyelash, eyebrow and he remembers hitting him like that. But we didn't sleep any more that night. So the next day was Valentine's Day. And again they're looking for two volunteers to walk across this big rice paddy, thousand yards, with a, and in the middle of it is this huge American rifle. Do you know the difference between a rifle and a cannon? I don't. Unless the rifle has riflings in the barrel. Any way, this is a really big gun and a week before when we were at Parinokway, we were watching American carrier planes come in and they were bombing Fort McKinley. Some of them were dropping parachute bombs and we could see the parachute open. But we did see one American plane that had to break formation from the planes on either side and he just never made it. He hit into Manila Bay. They probably rescued him. But any way, they wanted two guys, me and Frank, to go to the railroad track.

Seems like they were going to shoot at us. Okay. So we walked out and we were going to get past this big gun and he said, well, let's go inside and see if there's any what we call mandarin oranges. The Japs should have surrendered long ago. Whatever food they had, it was canned and there was something called fish and beans. You had to be starving to eat that. So we knew the code numbers for the mandarin oranges which we called tangerine sections. There were none in there. But there was a toy in there. It was the gun itself, there were two seats and we each sat in one seat and we turned these wheels and one made the thing traverse and the other wheel made it elevated. So we're having fun, we are doing that, we're going all the way around, you know. But it had a consequence.

So that was enough playing. We got out and finished our walk to the railroad track, didn't see anything, nobody shot at us, we go back, we got back in, we are sitting there and playing and that's enough. We get out, we are walking like the last good hundred yards and there comes a company commander and our platoon leader, a little bandy rooster he was and some other guys. We thought, hey, we're going to get a commendation like at least for what we did, medals and all of that. When they got close we saw they had fire and anger in their eyes. They said, you know what you just did? When they saw that gun going around, and nobody else knew that you were in there, everybody else thought that the Japs had re occupied that gun. We had called and alerted the Battalion 81 millimeter mortars, the Division artillery and the Air Force and they were getting ready to bomb that thing. Sort of stupid.

So, all right, now we get to the battle of Fort McKinley, February 15, 1945. The morning dawned nice and bright. Why does the Army have to start a battle in the morning? Couldn't they wait an hour or two? Why must we go into the sun, you know, and why didn't they wait for the tank? So we were properly dispersed and the first guys get up to the railroad track and they are waiting for more guys to get there and then all of a sudden they say, go. And one of our guys, Dan Haligan (ph), always used to have a saying, whatever we did, he would say, this is it. And so when he went over the train embankment, he says, this is really it.

So there's two words you have to learn, one of them is deathalade (ph), a defile, that's like a tire track could be a defile. When you are being shelled or shot at, you are looking for any one inch advantage to get your butt down there a little bit lower out of the line of fire. So there wasn't much defile there. But on the left we were really getting shot at, the first squad. On the right, they were on the other side of a little hill and so they were in deathalade and they were able to advance and that's where I saw Emmanuel Perez win the Medal of Honor.

He was able to go up on the right. So we get over the hill or over the railroad track and guys are getting shot left and right, but not killed. The difference between the Japanese 25s and our American, the 30 caliber is the difference between getting punched by your five year old nephew and by Joe Louis. If you get hit with our American 30 caliber, you get hit in the arm, it tears your arm off or destroys all the bones. The Jap 25, it would just stick right in your flesh or in the bone and you could carry on, you could walk or do anything. So that's why we lost a lot of guys wounded but not killed.

So this Bob Pelster who I said was an all city basketball player in Chicago, I don't know if you could ever say one person lost more than the rest but I don't know maybe if a pianist was shot through his hand, maybe he lost more than me who couldn't do any of that. But Bobby was shot through the forearm and it came out his elbow and he had a real promising future as a basketball player and he was built like Joe Palooka in the comics, really, what do you call it, big wide shoulders tapered down to about a 32 waist.

He just died in the last year or two. So we gave him a shot of morphine from his little pack there, took him back over the railroad track. And then that's where our medic got shot. And we took him back but medics don't carry rifles. So we could not do the universal sign of wounded laying here which is, you take, put the bayonet on the rifle and stick it upside down, if you have time maybe you tie your handkerchief on there. So it wasn't until -- I have to preface everything with this. I have no idea of time. I don't know whether this battle took an hour or four hours. And I've tried to think of it and there's no reference points.

So any way, we put him in the shade and then later that day in the afternoon guys who had taken the wounded back, we'd say, how's this guy, how's that guy, then somebody asked, how's the medic. Well, we didn't see him. Somebody said, what if he's still by those trees. Well, he was lying out there all that time but by now the sun was on him and he died later that day. So that was pretty sad because he was a good kid.

So we started going up the hill, shooting, throwing hand grenades in the big, there was the big pill box with logs on top and then a half a dozen smaller ones, open top. So I'm halfway up the hill and I look and I see my buddy Bill from Jamestown, New York, he's leaning up against, sitting with his back up against another pill box and he's sort of holding his leg. So I ran over to him, I let the battle go a minute, I ran over to him and here's this Jap officer. Now, this Jap officer was a naval officer with that nice black uniform with the gold piping and buttons and he's crawling toward Bill out in the open, everybody can see him, you know, nobody's getting hurt and this Jap has his sword, he's crawling on the ground, he's got his sword and Bill says, get me that sword, and I says, let me take care of your leg.

So we cut his pants leg open and his whole cast fell into my hand like that. Is there such a thing as a flank steak? A big chunk of steak, I was holding that in my hand. I says, give me your belt or something and we tied it up, gave him a shot of morphine. He says, get me that goddamn sword. So just then somebody from the third platoon is running up and they see this Jap and they look at me and at Bill and they say, is he bothering you? And they said, yeah, so he just went boom, shot the Japanese officer in the head. Is that an international law?

Well, any way, we dragged the guy over and the next thing that happened, mortar shells were landing and mortar makes this sound when it is shooting (indicating) and we said, that one's coming in and there was Birdie Hill as close as I am to my car, if he had had a baseball glove, he could have caught that. It was that close to him, as close as I am to you, that mortar shell went off and I told Bill, I says, Birdie, Birdie Hill was his name, Birdie got hit, I swear it hit him right in the head.

Next thing you know, the dust clears and Birdie Hill who looked like Harry Truman, was sitting up and he gave me the thumbs up. By that time, Manuel Perez had run up on that side and I could remember him jumping up on this one open top pill box and firing down into it and then running further. But that's the furthest advance I saw of anybody that day.

In the meantime, somebody had thrown a grenade in the back of the big pill box and everybody was in, everybody in there was dead. So I went up and, you know, wanted further orders, what should I do to my sergeant and this Lieutenant Covert (ph). By the way, to me Lieutenant Covert was the hero of that battle because when we were going up over the railroad track and really being shot at, he says, move forward, I don't care if you move two feet, but get up and move. So, you know, if you are going to move two feet, you might as well move ten feet looking for that piece of deathalade.

So one corporal -- by then we were all sergeants, the sergeant comes up to him and says, Lieutenant, let's get off of this hill, we're getting the shit kicked out of us. He says, we're not moving, if we have to dig in, we will. We bought this hill with blood, sort of a dramatic cliche, no? Maybe he saw some John Wayne movie. But he did say that, he says, we bought this hill with blood, we're not moving.

So by then somebody else had got shot and I bet I helped carry at least four guys, threw them in the poncho, grabbed the four corners, four guys, grabbed each a corner and by then we knew the other side was in deathalade, so at least we got them over there, sometimes we took them down the hill another ten, 20 yards then up, back we came and we would barely start talking to our officers and then boom, couple of more guys, so out they went.

So about the third time I went up, we're talking to the lieutenant and the sergeants and right between us the lieutenant got hit right in the chest. But again, all it did was knock him over and I don't think he had one of those bulletproof bibles you always hear guys getting shot in the bible. But he fell over, he got knocked over and the first thing he said was, I'm hit, give me my wife's picture. So we let him know about that after he came back after being wounded.

So Frank and I and maybe Bill Steins or Mutener or somebody, we carried him out. And he had been on our ass for a year and a half but we gave him ample reason to be picking on us and getting in minor trouble, yeah. But any way, so we carried him out because we really admired him. But before he was moved, he called Sergeant DuFresne over and he says, Sergeant, I'm giving you a battlefield commission. And this is the guy whose serial number ended in 1776. I think he knew more about Army history and stuff than ten officers put together.

So, and then Lieutenant Covert said, Sergeant McGuire, who was my sergeant, you're going to be the platoon sergeant. That's how I made sergeant, by default. They had to ask three guys before me. They said, this was later that day, we need a sergeant. So by default, I won, yeah. So any way, I came back and Lieutenant DuFresne, yeah, Sergeant DuFresne says, I says, what do you want me to do? He says, well, advance, see what's behind those pill boxes.

So the second platoon medic was sitting with his back to the pill box and he was ministering to somebody, bandaging somebody, wounded, lying next to him and you talk about luck, I had to run from here to the garage and as I'm running, I have to tell you that when a bullet is fired at you, you know the difference, you know the difference between a bullet fired at you and one fired two feet from you. When you're on the rifle range as a rookie, you can tell and you're in the pit operating those targets that go up and down, you can tell which bullet was fired toward your target.

You can't see but it has a different sound. And as I'm running, I heard that sound, that bullet was for me. I dove and landed on Medic Parker's shins, maybe the top of my head was near his knee and that bullet hit him above the knee two inches and he lost his leg later. So that was a close shave. So then we took him out, we came back and Sergeant DuFresne said the two words, there's two phrases you never want to hear in the Army. One of them is incoming for artillery and the other is fixed bayonets. That means you are going to go look somebody in the eyeball. And don't write this down, but I don't think that these soldiers that are going to the Gulf now, I don't call them heroes. A hero is somebody that can, where the enemy has a 50-50 chance of killing him. These kids are just going there, they are not being shot at.

We drop bombs from 20,000 feet, we don't see the kids that get hurt or killed. You can tell I'm a peace activist. So any way, he says, we've just realized we're getting most of the fire or all the fire now. It's from the left down on the road. So he says, Sergeant McGuire, take four guys and you're going to run down, fixed bayonets and run down and find those guys.We drop bombs from 20,000 feet, we don't see the kids that get hurt or killed. You can tell I'm a peace activist. SIn the meantime, Sergeant Murphy, mortar sergeant, he asked him, how many rounds do you have and he says five. He says, start shooting them down there by the road but, he says, send somebody to get a couple of rounds from another platoon but don't shoot them, just five. So we fixed bayonets and two are going to go this way and two are going to start from that side of this big pill box and the two machine guns are going to be set up and they are going to be covering us while we run down the hill. So we're just getting ready to -- I'm almost done.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, that's okay.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Ralph Mutener (ph), he said this a hundred times. He says, wait a minute, wait a minute. He says, do you know who I am? I was first in my class in communications school. He says, I'm authorized to do wig-wag, semaphores, putting out colored panels, dot-dash, repair radios and stuff, he says, why am I here, why am I in the infantry?

And we said, yeah, Ralph, we heard that. And then Frank says, wait a minute, wait a minute, he says, Sarge, for two years I have been hearing about something called a rebel yell. He says, can you give us a rebel yell to get started? Sergeant says, you know, let's go.

So we got all lined up and motioned to the machine guns, don't just waste all your, the whole belt, you know, a few shots at a time and don't shoot us in the back of the head. So they start shooting and we start running and, you know, we're facing, how can I say that, we're on the wrong side of the hill. We're facing them, they are like shooting up into the stands of a football stadium.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you are going down?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: We're going down the hill. I had a thought there. Oh, we decided, why stop, you know, why stop and assume that, you know, the knee position or something, just go. So we started going, shot a couple of times at nothing. And the next thing you know, the Japs did a very dumb thing, they got out of the hole and ran up the road.

Well, our machine gun just picked them off. So the war was over, that battle was over and I can not tell you how long it lasted. Then the next thing we did was loot the bodies and we knew they were not booby trapped yet. So we cut off all of the shoulder patches, reached inside their helmets that had those nice silk white flags with the orange ball in there, the rising sun.

And then we heard a strange sound, real, like a bunch of iron clanking together and we looked around and back from where we came, there's the tank, here comes a US Army tank. And by then everybody had hollered, you know, cease fire and it was very quiet. So we went back up the hill and one of the jobs we had was pick up all of the rifles and cartridge belts and anything that's, you know, useful.

So we did and we took that back over to the railroad track, get there. Nobody was in a hurry and the tank guys, the tank commander is talking to one of our lieutenants and he is just showing him, well, you know, we were just across the railroad tracks here and we were going to go farther on but as long as you're here. So there were about ten guys, infantrymen, with the tank. Well, they went down there over the railroad tracks and that's the last we saw of them. Where were they, you know, three hours before or nine o'clock in the morning? I think the whole battle would have been different. Questions, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind that you haven't covered that's not necessarily related to what you talked about?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: To that? Okay, one on Leyte, our C Company was ambushed by the Japs, they were protecting a hospital way out in the jungle, but when I say jungle, this was at five or 10,000 feet and yet it was jungle flora. Yeah, I wish we had at least seen a monkey when we were so hungry because those hillbillies knew how to cook all of that. A vivid memory?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Okay. When we were going up to where we were going to assault this hospital, I didn't go on that one, we stayed up here. The third platoon went down and got shot up. But as we were going there we passed two dead guys. One was Ernie, he was the C Company barber. And our job later was to bury him and these trees had all those big -- what do you call those trees in Florida where the roots are in the water?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I know what you are talking about.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: Not cypress, there's another kind, banyan?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: We just had our entrenching shovels, we couldn't dig a decent hole. So we dug this -- no, Ernie, we just put him in the roots of this tree, you know. He was like sitting up nice and we used handfuls and shovelfuls of dirt until we covered him and I suppose somebody had to make a map to show where he was and the grave registration came after the fighting was over and dug up these guys.

But the other lieutenant, we called him Harry James because he looked like Harry James. You remember him? According to best infantry school procedure, when the maybe somebody got shot first, he ran up behind this huge log that was across the path, the trail. Well, in all kinds of training, when, you know, the scouts see those cardboard figures, that's the enemy, they call up the lieutenant and he hides behind the bush and he goes like that and he sees what has to be done, two of you guys go that way and two of you go this way and set up the machine gun, perfect, except the cardboard targets don't shoot back. So this guy ran up and he must have ducked down and he could have crawled under that fallen log.

But instead he does this, and from about 25 feet away they got him right in the forehead. So we buried him. But again, we couldn't make it a six foot long. So we put him in the hole and his head was sort of sticking out like it was on a pillow. So Nick says, wait a minute. He just jumped on his chest and he fit in the hole, it was a perfect fit. So that's a vivid memory.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did you get the Silver Star?

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: That's another, that's a long story but I'll tell you half of it. You don't have to write that. Some other time I will or I'll even bring you the citation which is not exactly correct. Don't believe any citation.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've learned that.

sp.speaker: Steve M. Hegedus
sp.p: I had yellow jaundice. I had never dropped out of one single march but here as we're walking up and down these hills, southern Luzon checking out all these hills for caves or something, I couldn't make it, I couldn't walk, I had to stop and rest while everybody went past me. And then about a day or two later, I'm peeing Coca-Cola and I says, that doesn't look right. And some old hillbilly guy says, boy, you got the "jaunders". Yeah, so I was really sick. So we reached the top of this, it was only a knob of a hill, nothing big, maybe half the size of a football field. And old sarge says -- oh, that's the first time we ever saw a BAR.

We received some replacements and this one kid had a BAR. Hey, come on, we want to see that thing work. We saw what we thought were caves about a hundred yards away so he set the thing up and he fired some tracers into the cave. And you know, those Japs were amazing. They could dig a hole and leave no evidence. That's sort of the end of that campaign.
